world_behind.title: The road south
world_behind.text: From Jerusalem to "the borders near the shore of the Red Sea" (v. 5) is roughly a hundred and eighty miles of hard country, then "three days in the wilderness" (v. 6) beyond. A household moving that route with tents, provisions, and women needed desert skill and speed. The record does not say where Lehi learned the roads. It does say why the family was in a hurry: "they seek to take away thy life" (v. 1).

world_behind.title: What an inheritance meant
world_behind.text: Land in Judah was ancestral allotment, held in the family name for generations. Walking away from "the land of his inheritance" (v. 4) was a kind of social death, and the brothers' bill of grievance (v. 11) lists the property in exactly the order the record lists what Lehi abandoned.

cites.quote: the land of his inheritance

spans.text: the land of his inheritance

world_behind.title: Tents were wealth and skill
world_behind.text: "My father dwelt in a tent" (v. 15) compresses a way of life: tents were costly equipment, and living from them required practiced desert craft. The family did not stumble into the wilderness; it was outfitted for it.

cites.quote: My father dwelt in a tent

spans.text: My father dwelt in a tent

world_behind.title: An altar away from the temple
world_behind.text: Lehi "built an altar of stones, and made an offering" (v. 7) far from Jerusalem's sanctuary. The old law itself provided for rough stone altars (Ex. 20:25), and the patriarchs built them at their camps along the road (Gen. 12:8). Whatever the era's temple politics, the record presents a patriarch acting in an older, travel-worn pattern of worship.

cites.quote: built an altar of stones, and made an offering

spans.text: built an altar of stones, and made an offering

world_behind.title: Naming as claiming and teaching
world_behind.text: Fathers in the ancient Near East named wells, camps, and children to fix meaning to a place. Lehi names a desert river and a valley after two sons. If the river was a seasonal wadi, the wish that Laman run "continually" (v. 9) into the sea is sharper still: desert rivers quit.

cites.quote: continually

spans.text: continually

world_behind.title: The eldest son's expectations
world_behind.text: Laman stood first in line under every custom of the age. The promise that a younger brother would be "a ruler and a teacher over thy brethren" (v. 22) cuts against everything he expected to inherit, and the record will spend centuries on the resentment. Scripture's older stories ran the same way, from Jacob to Joseph to David: the younger is chosen, and the household lives with it.

cites.quote: a ruler and a teacher over thy brethren

spans.text: a ruler and a teacher over thy brethren

words.text: Stones piled where a family stopped walking. Lehi "built an altar of stones, and made an offering unto the Lord" (v. 7) before anything else happens in the valley. The record names an altar four times in a thousand years, against three hundred and seventy-eight in the King James Bible, and the scarcity measures the distance from a temple. Worship in this chapter is portable, built by hand, and left behind when the tents move.

cites.quote: built an altar of stones, and made an offering unto the Lord

spans.text: built an altar of stones, and made an offering unto the Lord

words.text: The record's word for complaint enters here, and it is a precise one: murmuring is under-the-breath speech, resistance that never risks open argument. Laman and Lemuel "did murmur in many things against their father" (v. 11). They talked about him where he could not answer. The diagnosis follows a verse later, and the word will follow this family across the sea.

cites.quote: did murmur in many things against their father

spans.text: did murmur in many things against their father

words.text: On the brothers' lips, "a visionary man" (v. 11) is a dismissal: a dreamer, unfit to steer a family's fortunes. The record lets the insult stand until Lehi picks it up himself and wears it as a title (1 Ne. 5:4). One word, two theologies: what the sons call delusion, the father calls sight.

cites.quote: a visionary man

spans.text: a visionary man

words.text: An ox that will not turn under the yoke. The prophets' old word for Israel (Ex. 32:9) is applied by Nephi to his own brothers. The nation's ailment is diagnosed inside one tent, before the family has been gone a week.

Lehi speaks "with power" (v. 14) until his sons' "frames did shake" (v. 14) and they "durst not utter against him" (v. 14). To confound is to overwhelm speech itself: the murmuring stops because words failed. Nothing in the scene says a mind changed, and compliance won by confounding lasts exactly until the next chapter of trouble.

cites.quote: with power

spans.text: with power

cites.quote: frames did shake

spans.text: frames did shake

cites.quote: durst not utter against him

spans.text: durst not utter against him

words.text: Nephi's conversion verb. He cried out, and the Lord "did soften my heart that I did believe" (v. 16). Softening is something done to him, at his asking, not something he achieved. Set against "the hardness of their hearts" (v. 18) two verses later, the chapter offers one variable to explain two sons of the same father.

cites.quote: did soften my heart that I did believe

spans.text: did soften my heart that I did believe

cites.quote: the hardness of their hearts

spans.text: the hardness of their hearts

phrases.text: The Lord speaks to Lehi "even in a dream" (v. 1), and says it again in the next verse (v. 2). After the fire and the open vision of the first chapter, the instructions that save the family arrive in sleep. The record does not rank the two. Lehi obeys a dream exactly as he obeyed the pillar of fire.

cites.quote: even in a dream

spans.text: even in a dream

phrases.text: Verse 4 is built on two lists. What he left: house, inheritance, gold, silver, precious things. What he took: family, provisions, tents. The sentence does the arithmetic of discipleship without a word of comment, and the brothers will keep the first list alive as an accusation (v. 11) for the rest of their lives.

phrases.term: O that thou mightest be like
phrases.text: The naming wishes come as a matched pair, river for Laman and valley for Lemuel, and both open with longing: "O that thou mightest be like unto this river" (v. 9). A father praying his sons into the landscape, choosing for one the image of constancy in motion and for the other constancy in place. The grammar admits what a command would hide: this is hope, and hope can fail.

cites.quote: O that thou mightest be like unto this river

spans.text: O that thou mightest be like unto this river

phrases.term: The foolish imaginations of his heart
phrases.text: The brothers' theory of their father, stated once and held for decades. They will repeat it, barely altered, on the far shore of the world (1 Ne. 17:20). The phrase is the counter-thesis to the whole record: where Nephi writes revelation, Laman reads imagination.

phrases.term: Inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments ye shall prosper
phrases.text: The covenant formula of the entire volume enters the record here, spoken to a young man in a tent. "Inasmuch as" is exact grammar: blessing in the measure of obedience, no more, no less. Lehi will restate it to his sons (2 Ne. 1:20), and the small-plates historians will still be checking history against it centuries on (Jarom 1:9).

phrases.term: Cut off from the presence of the Lord
phrases.text: The formula's dark half. Not destruction but distance: presence is the blessing, absence the curse. The record will report its fulfillment in those same words within a generation (2 Ne. 5:20), and the phrase keeps its precision all the way down the book.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: A household roster with the writer left out of it
verses.text: The record names the party: "my mother, Sariah, and my elder brothers, who were Laman, Lemuel, and Sam." Nephi is not in his own list, and no daughters are named, although 2 Nephi 5:6 will later mention "my sisters" as part of the group that leaves with him. The roster is thus incomplete on both counts, and the record never corrects it. Sariah is named four times in the whole record, here and at 1 Nephi 5:1, 5:6, and 8:14, and never after 1 Nephi 8.

verses.label: v. 8–10
verses.title: A river and a valley named, then preached at
verses.text: The record has the naming and the sermon happen in the same breath. The river is called Laman at verse 8, and at verse 9 the son of that name is told, "O that thou mightest be like unto this river, continually running into the fountain of all righteousness." The valley carries Lemuel's name, and the address at verse 10 asks for the valley's qualities, "firm and steadfast, and immovable." A feature is named after a man and then held up as what the man is not.

chapter.title: Obedience told at speed
chapter.text: Command (v. 2), summary (v. 3), and departure (v. 4) take three verses, with no scene of deliberation between them. "He was obedient unto the word of the Lord" (v. 3) is the whole account of Lehi's decision. The pacing is the point: the record measures the man by the shortness of the gap between hearing and going.

cites.quote: He was obedient unto the word of the Lord

spans.text: He was obedient unto the word of the Lord

chapter.title: A family splits on one question
chapter.text: Everything divides over whether "Jerusalem, that great city, could be destroyed" (v. 13). The brothers' unbelief is confidence in permanence, and Nephi ties it to the city's own mood: they were "like unto the Jews" (v. 13). The volume's thousand-year conflict begins here as a disagreement in a tent.

cites.quote: Jerusalem, that great city, could be destroyed

spans.text: Jerusalem, that great city, could be destroyed

cites.quote: like unto the Jews

spans.text: like unto the Jews

chapter.title: The wilderness as first classroom
chapter.text: The chapter puts the physical feature first and the lesson second, three times. Verse 6 pitches a tent in a valley by a river; verse 7 builds "an altar of stones" and gives thanks; verses 9 and 10 turn the river and the valley into two addresses, "O that thou mightest be like unto this river" and "like unto this valley, firm and steadfast." Verse 11 then names the reason the sermons were needed. The pattern of terrain first and doctrine drawn from it holds through the broken bow at 1 Nephi 16:18–31 and the ship at 1 Nephi 17:8–11.

chapter.title: The handoff at verse 16
chapter.text: The chapter opens inside Lehi's dream and ends inside Nephi's covenant. Verse 15's one-line tent notice is the hinge: the father's account closes on what he has left, and the son steps forward wanting to know. From here the record runs on Nephi's experience, with Lehi seen from outside.

chapter.title: The covenant before the nation
chapter.text: Verses 20–24 hand a teenager the constitutional terms of two peoples not yet born: prosper, be cut off, rule, be scourged, remember. The record's editors will spend the rest of the volume checking events against these five verses, and the chapter's placement means every reader knows the terms before meeting the history.

chapter.title: Second panel of the departure unit
chapter.text: Chapter 1 announced the city's doom; this chapter obeys it. The two returns that follow, for the record (chs. 3–4) and for the family (ch. 7), will send the sons back over this same road, testing them against the standard of quick obedience their father set here.

chapter.title: Murmuring gets a diagnosis
chapter.text: The record could have left the brothers as villains; instead verse 12 explains them: "they knew not the dealings of that God who had created them" (v. 12). Unbelief is framed as ignorance of God's character, a knowledge problem before it is a loyalty problem, which is why the remedy throughout the book is always recital: remember, remember the dealings.

cites.quote: they knew not the dealings of that God who had created them

spans.text: they knew not the dealings of that God who had created them

applications.title: Close the gap between hearing and going
applications.text: Lehi's obedience is measured in the verse-count between command and departure. Pick the one commandment you have been deliberating instead of doing, and let the deliberation end this week; the feelings can catch up on the road.

applications.title: Build the altar at the first stop
applications.text: Thanksgiving placed at the start of hardship changes the character of the whole journey. In the current wilderness, whether new job, new ward, or new diagnosis, make the first deliberate act one of thanks and mark it in some way you can return to.

applications.title: Speak wishes over people, out loud
applications.text: Lehi blesses in the grammar of longing, tied to what is in front of him. Choose one person and one concrete image, something they can see again, and say the wish to them plainly. Longing spoken is not weakness; it is how a father prays in public.

applications.title: Study the dealings
applications.text: The murmurers' deficit was biographical: they did not know how God deals. The countermeasure is history: scripture's record and your own. Trace one past dealing of God with your family far enough to tell it well.

applications.title: Ask for the softening
applications.text: Nephi did not harden himself into faith; he cried out and was softened. When belief is thin, the working prayer is not "make the doctrine easier" but "soften me toward it," a prayer the chapter shows being answered.

applications.title: Turn grief into intercession
applications.text: When his brothers refused his words, Nephi's next act was to cry to the Lord for them. For the person whose hardness currently grieves you, trade one conversation about them for one prayer for them, and keep the trade going.

questions.text: If the command came today, what would be on my leaving list, and which item would I mourn longest?
Which piece of the world in front of me would a wise parent turn into a wish for me, and what weakness would it aim at?
Which of God's dealings, in scripture or in my own family, do I actually know well enough to retell?
What is my tent: the reduced, sufficient thing I could actually live from if the first list vanished?
When did I last cry unto the Lord for belief itself, rather than drifting on the belief I inherited?
The Lord names both diligence and lowliness in Nephi's seeking. Which half is thinner in mine?
Has any scourge in my life ever stirred me to remembrance, and did I let it finish the work?
